prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the temperature from an LM75 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, performs the read once per second, stores each reading in an in‑memory circular buffer of capacity 60 samples protected by a mutex, updates a running average from the buffer, and drives an alert LED connected to GPIO18 (BCM) from a background thread so that the LED is turned on whenever the temperature exceeds 28.0 °C and turned off otherwise; the implementation must check the result of every I2C read/write and every GPIO initialization call, log any sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions to stderr, attempt to re‑initialize the hardware on such errors, and ensure that on all exit paths—including normal termination, error paths, and receipt of SIGINT—the program cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C file descriptor, releasing the GPIO line, and destroying the mutex.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that regulates a resistive heater with a PID loop using a PT100 RTD read through a MAX31865 on SPI0 CE0 configured to mode 1 at 500 kHz, employing a 430‑ohm reference resistor and assuming the PT100 nominal resistance of 100 Ω, where the heater is driven by a MOSFET controlled with hardware PWM on GPIO18 at a 1 kHz frequency using a driver range of 1000 for 0‑100 % duty; the PID loop must execute every 100 ms, loading the target temperature and PID gains from a JSON configuration file at startup with defaults of 25 °C, Kp = 1.0, Ki = 0.1, Kd = 0.01 if any values are missing, and must implement a failsafe that immediately sets the PWM duty to zero and exits with an error if the temperature exceeds 80 °C, an SPI read fails, or any MAX31865 fault is detected, while also handling SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by turning off the heater, closing the SPI interface, terminating the driver, and exiting cleanly, and logging any errors to stderr and returning a non‑zero exit code on critical failures.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a BMP180 sensor on the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1, sampling once per second, and writes any temperature reading above 30.0 °C or pressure reading below 950 hPa to a file named breach_log.txt with a timestamp for each breach; the program must perform all BMP180 calibration calculations using integer arithmetic only, avoid any floating‑point pow operations, check the result of every system call and retry transient failures up to three times, explicitly handle cases where the sensor is absent or the I2C bus reports an error, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples a BMP180 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, reading and validating the 11‑word calibration table from the documented register before any sampling, and then, via a hardware timer callback that fires every 500 ms, obtains temperature and pressure using the BMP180 formulas with OSS = 0 (ensuring the temperature routine is not called from inside the pressure routine), stores each timestamped reading in a 60‑entry circular buffer, prints each new reading to stdout, and drives a cooling fan connected to GPIO18 (active‑high) whenever the temperature exceeds 30 °C; the timer callback must remain simple and avoid blocking calls, every library API call’s return code must be checked and the sample skipped on error, and the program must handle SIGINT/SIGTERM by turning the fan off, closing the I2C handle, and invoking the library’s cleanup API call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces to a BMP180 sensor on the I2C bus using the documented address, reads the sensor’s calibration data and applies the Bosch compensation formulas to compute pressure in pascals, and toggles data logging on and off via a falling‑edge interrupt on GPIO27 with a 200 ms debounce; while logging is enabled the program must record a timestamp and the computed pressure to a file named pressure_log.txt every 2 seconds, must detect and recover from I2C communication errors and driver initialization failures, and must clean up all allocated resources and gracefully terminate when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier on SPI0 using CE0 (GPIO8 as chip‑select, GPIO9 MISO, GPIO10 MOSI, GPIO11 SCLK) at 2 MHz, drives a solid‑state relay connected to GPIO17 with a PWM signal to modulate a resistive heater so that a PI controller with anti‑windup maintains a target temperature (default 25.0 °C) while never exceeding a safe maximum duty cycle of 80 %, logs each measurement and the applied duty cycle together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named heater_log.csv, and implements error handling such that any SPI read failure or any MAX31855 fault condition (open circuit, short to ground or VCC) causes the duty cycle to be set immediately to 0 % and the error to be recorded in the log while the program continues running, and also catches SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that turns off the heater, closes the SPI interface, closes the log file, and terminates the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls the CPU temperature every 0.5 seconds and drives a common‑anode RGB LED attached to the GPIO bus with the Red cathode on GPIO17, Green cathode on GPIO18 and Blue cathode on GPIO27, using hardware PWM via the library’s API call() with a 0‑255 range and inverted duty (255 turns the channel off) while respecting the 3.3 V common‑anode supply and individual current‑limiting resistors; the program must open the temperature file, check the return value of the API call() each time it sets a PWM value and on any failure print an error message and exit with a non‑zero status, also handling fopen failure and short or failed reads by checking ferror, printing a diagnostic and skipping that update cycle, and on each loop iteration print to stdout the temperature in millidegrees Celsius together with the three PWM values; the LED color should be solid Blue (0,0,255) for temperatures below 40000 m°C, solid Green (0,255,0) for 40000‑59999 m°C, and solid Red (255,0,0) for 60000 m°C and above; a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, turn off all channels by writing a duty of 255, call the library’s API call() for cleanup, and allow the main loop to exit gracefully without calling exit() inside the handler, ensuring the file handle is closed on every code path and the program runs an infinite loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads humidity and temperature from a DHT22 sensor connected on the 1‑wire bus with its data line on GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7), using the required start signal of pulling the line low for at least 1 ms, then captures the full 40‑bit response, validates the 8‑bit checksum, and posts the measured values as a JSON payload to http://yourserver.com/api/humidity via HTTP; the implementation must gracefully handle cases where the sensor is absent, checksum mismatches, and network errors by retrying up to three times, and must ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses I2C bus 1 to communicate with a BMP180 sensor, configuring the sensor for oversampling setting OSS=3 and applying the full Bosch BMP180 integer‑only compensation algorithm, and that toggles data logging on and off with a push‑button connected to GPIO 4 configured for falling‑edge interrupts with the internal pull‑up; the interrupt handler must debounce using a driver‑library tick comparison of at least 200 000 µs, and when logging is enabled the program shall read pressure every 2 seconds, waiting the required 26 ms conversion delay, and append a timestamped pressure value in hPa to a file named pressure_log.txt, while printing a status message when logging is disabled; the code must check every I2C read/write return value, report any errors to stderr, fail cleanly if the sensor is absent or returns invalid calibration data, and on receipt of SIGINT must close the I2C handle and release all driver resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads humidity from a DHT22 sensor connected on the 1‑wire bus using GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7) by issuing the start signal (pull the data line low for at least 1 ms, then high for 20‑40 µs, then release), captures the 40‑bit response with microsecond‑level edge timing, validates the checksum and, if the sensor is absent or the checksum fails, retries up to three times with a 2‑second backoff before giving up; the main loop must perform a read every 10 seconds, and each successful reading must be formatted as JSON and POSTed with Content‑Type: application/json to http://your‑the‑library’s‑API‑call.com/api/humidity, retrying the POST up to three times on network or HTTP errors and treating any non‑2xx response as a failure; the program must initialize the driver library with the library’s API call() and check for errors, log all events to syslog, accept a command‑line option “-s <url>” to override the default URL, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a graceful shutdown that calls the library’s API call() and curl_global_cleanup() on every exit path.

Write a C program for the Raspberry Pi 5 that actively manages the official Raspberry Pi 5 Active Cooler by reading the CPU temperature from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp and the current fan state from /sys/class/thermal/cooling_device0/cur_state, polling the temperature every 5 seconds, applying a tiered speed map where temperatures below 45 °C set the fan state to 0 (off), below 55 °C set state 1, below 65 °C set state 2, and 65 °C or higher set state 3 (maximum), first validating the cooling device’s max_state before any write, and writing the new state back to the same cooling_device sysfs entry only when the speed changes; each fan speed change must be logged with a timestamp to /var/log/fan_control.log, all file opens, reads, writes, and parses must be checked for errors with transient read failures simply causing the program to retry on the next cycle, and the program must handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by setting the fan to state 0, logging the shutdown event, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements a PID controller to maintain a target temperature of 50 °C by PWM‑controlling a resistive heater on GPIO18 using hardware PWM at 1 kHz with a duty range of 0‑100 %; the program must read the current temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier connected on SPI0 (CLK = GPIO11, CS = GPIO8/CE0, DO = GPIO9) at 500 kHz, acquiring 4 bytes per sample, and log every second to a file named heater_log.txt the measured temperature, the PWM duty cycle, and the PID output; the PID defaults are Kp = 1.0, Ki = 0.1, Kd = 0.01, and the controller must include error handling that parses the MAX31855 fault bits to detect open‑circuit, short‑to‑GND, or short‑to‑VCC conditions, logs any such errors, disables the heater and resets the PID state, and also enforces a failsafe that disables the heater if the reading exceeds 100 °C or falls below 0 °C; finally, the program must cleanly release resources on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the heater off, closing the SPI interface, and terminating any driver activity.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the GPIO bus to drive the PWM input of a Noctua NF‑A4x10 5V PWM fan connected to GPIO18 (physical pin 12), polling the CPU temperature every 5 seconds and mapping the temperature linearly to a 25 kHz PWM duty cycle where temperatures of 40 °C and below correspond to 0 % duty, 70 °C and above correspond to 100 % duty, and values in between are interpolated accordingly; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, confirm that each PWM frequency and duty cycle call succeeds, and log each reading to a file named cooling_log.csv with a header and rows containing the timestamp, temperature in °C, and the PWM duty cycle percentage, while also handling any file I/O errors, and it must clean up gracefully on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the fan off and releasing all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with two Sensirion SLF3S-1300F liquid flow sensors on I2C bus 1, assuming the sensors are attached through a Sensirion SF06 multiplexer breakout or a comparable I2C hub, and polls each sensor once per second, reading three bytes from each (two data bytes followed by a CRC‑8 byte) while validating the checksum and retrying up to three times on any I2C error before giving up on that read; when a valid reading is obtained, the program must append a line to flow_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,flow1,flow2”, skipping the entry if the CRC check fails, and it must handle a clean shutdown on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by closing all I2C handles and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a magnetic rotary encoder built from two TMAG5110A1 Hall‑Effect latch sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with Channel A wired to GPIO17 and Channel B to GPIO18, configuring the pins as open‑drain outputs with internal pull‑up resistors enabled, implementing a 2‑bit quadrature state machine that resolves 360 pulses per revolution into a normalized angular position ranging from 0.00 to 360.00 degrees, logging each timestamped position change to a file named encoder_log.txt, providing robust error handling for both GPIO initialization and file I/O operations, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released when the program receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal by using the driver library’s cleanup facilities.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with the Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, samples the sensor every 100 ms, and logs each measurement to a CSV file named adpd144ri_log.txt with columns timestamp, red, and ir; the program must also monitor the infrared reading and activate an LED connected to GPIO17 (active‑high) whenever the IR value exceeds a threshold of 2000, while robustly handling I2C read/write errors and conditions where the sensor is absent, and it must cleanly release all resources—including the I2C file descriptor, GPIO lines, and the log file—on any exit path by catching SIGINT and SIGTERM signals for graceful shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the RPM from a Melexis MLX90254 magnetic speed sensor by counting its pulses on the GPIO bus, using GPIO18 (physical pin 12) configured as an input with a pull‑down resistor, counting only rising edges and assuming one pulse per revolution; the program must calculate the RPM over a 1‑second interval, protect the pulse counter with a pthread mutex shared between the interrupt service routine and the main thread, log each RPM value together with a timestamp to rpm_log.txt in append mode flushing the file immediately, include error handling that checks the driver library initialization, ISR registration, and log file opening, and install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that performs a graceful shutdown by terminating the driver library, closing the log file, and destroying the mutex, while also handling the case of a missing sensor by logging 0.00 RPM when no pulses are detected.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that communicates over I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1) with an Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor using the documented address, samples the sensor every 100 ms, logs each timestamped reading to a CSV file named adpd144ri_log.txt, and triggers an LED connected to GPIO17 whenever the infrared reading exceeds a threshold of 2000; the implementation must robustly handle I2C errors and the case where the sensor is absent, and must clean up all resources—including the I2C bus, GPIO lines, and the log file—on every exit path, also handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals, while avoiding any use of deprecated driver libraries or driver library components.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that samples the analog audio output of an Adafruit MAX9814 Electret Microphone Amplifier connected via GPIO, using the OUT pin (audio signal) on GPIO17 as an input and the GAIN select pin on GPIO18 as an output (set GPIO18 LOW to select 60 dB gain), polls the digital input every 10 ms to rapidly detect rising edges that indicate peak sound events, logs each detected event to a file named audio_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS LEVEL” where LEVEL is 1 for a rising edge, prints a startup message, and runs indefinitely until interrupted, while handling all driver library initialization and I/O errors robustly by checking the return value of every API call and ensuring clean release of all driver library resources on all exit paths through SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors the flow rate of a microfluidic drug delivery system using a Sensirion SLF3S‑4000B Liquid Flow Sensor connected to I2C bus 1, reading the sensor every 1000 ms by retrieving three bytes (a two‑byte MSB‑first raw value followed by a CRC‑8 byte that must be validated with the documented polynomial and initial value), logging each successful measurement to a CSV file named flow_log.csv in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,flow_rate_uL_min” with the file opened once at startup in append mode, kept open, and flushed after each write; the program must check driver initialization, I2C open, write, and read operations, log any I2C read/write failures to stderr and attempt recovery on the next loop iteration, log a CRC failure as an error and skip that reading, and on receipt of SIGINT cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and terminate the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with a Honeywell MICS‑VZ‑89TE VOC sensor on I2C bus 1, reads the sensor data, computes an indoor air quality (IAQ) index, and logs a timestamped line every 5 seconds to a CSV file named air_quality_log.csv containing the IAQ value together with TVOC in ppb and eCO₂ in ppm; the implementation must check every I2C read and write return value, detect and handle conditions where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error without crashing, and must also install a SIGINT handler that on receipt gracefully closes the I2C interface, flushes and closes the log file, and terminates the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously monitors a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s OUT line wired to GPIO 17 (BCM numbering, physical pin 11) as an input with the consumer label “ttp223_tamper”, polling the line every 100 ms based on CLOCK_MONOTONIC; the program must detect when the TTP223B output, which is HIGH while touched and LOW when released, remains continuously HIGH for more than 5 seconds, then print a single intrusion alert to stdout for that touch event and reset the timer when the sensor is released so that alerts are not repeated for the same touch, while checking every library call for failure and printing strerror(errno) on error, and if a sensor read fails mid‑loop printing an error and exiting with EXIT_FAILURE after performing cleanup; the cleanup routine must also be invoked on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM to gracefully release the line and close the chip on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously samples audio from an InvenSense INMP441 I2S MEMS microphone over the I2S bus using the Linux ALSA subsystem (e.g., /dev/snd/pcmC0D0c) and writes the 16‑bit PCM samples to a raw file named audio_capture.pcm, while driving the L/R channel‑select line on GPIO 17 (BCM) to select the left channel, and includes robust handling of I2S initialization failures, data acquisition errors, and file I/O problems together with proper resource release on all exit paths, including graceful termination when receiving a SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a SainSmart IR Flame Sensor Module (LM393 comparator with IR photodiode) connected via GPIO, reading the digital output (DO) on GPIO4 (BCM) every 50 ms and applying a 50 ms software debounce, and when the sensor output goes LOW indicating a flame, immediately start a hardware PWM signal at 100 Hz on GPIO18 (BCM) to drive a cooling fan, logging each event to a file named flame_log.txt with ISO‑8601 timestamps for system start, flame detection, flame end, and program shutdown; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver library, check the result of every GPIO read, detect a sensor‑absent condition by timing out if no valid reading is obtained, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly stop the PWM, reset the GPIO pins, terminate the driver library, and close the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TI AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor over SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8) configured at 1 MHz, mode 0, using a hardware frame trigger on GPIO23 (BCM) and a data‑ready interrupt on GPIO24 (BCM) to capture range‑Doppler heatmap frames at a 100 ms period; the sensor is pre‑configured via the TI mmWave SDK to stream range‑Doppler data, with a configuration struct that records a start frequency of 77 GHz, end frequency of 79 GHz, 64 chirps and 256 samples, and each frame requires a full‑duplex SPI transfer of 32 768 bytes of heatmap data, which must be logged to a binary file whose header contains the documented magic number 4144, an 8‑byte timestamp and the configuration struct, followed by per‑frame timestamps and frame numbers, while checking all return codes, handling any memory allocation failures, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM the program gracefully closes the SPI device, releases the GPIO pins and closes the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls the digital output of a KY‑026 Flame Sensor connected to GPIO20 (BCM) on the GPIO bus every 100 ms, detects when the sensor state changes between flame detected and flame cleared, and appends a line to a file named flame_log.txt containing an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp and the new state only on each transition; the implementation must verify the success of every driver call and every file‑I/O operation, explicitly handle the situation where the GPIO chip cannot be opened, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when the process receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with a Texas Instruments OPT3001 Ambient Light Sensor on I2C bus 1, configures the sensor for continuous conversion mode with automatic full‑scale range, reads lux values approximately every 100 ms conversion time, and appends each reading to a file named light_data.txt prefixed with an ISO‑8601 timestamp; the implementation must robustly handle I2C transaction failures and sensor‑absent conditions by retrying or logging errors without crashing, and must perform a clean shutdown on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by releasing the I2C bus handle, any driver resources, and closing all open file handles on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the SainSmart IR Flame Detection Sensor Module over the GPIO bus, requesting the flame sensor DOUT line as an input with a pulled‑up bias on GPIO line 17 (BCM, active‑low) using the driver library v2 API calls, and logs the status to the console once every second; each log entry must be formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” followed by “Flame Detected: YES” when the sensor value is 0 or “Flame Detected: NO” when the value is 1, while checking every driver library call and syscall for errors and printing clear error messages to stderr; the program must install a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag to break the main loop, and on cleanup it must release the line request, close the chip, and free all configuration and settings objects, and it must be compiled with gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 -o flame_detect flame_detect.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the Keywish KY‑033 3‑Way Tracing Sensor over GPIO, using GPIO17 (BCM) for the left output, GPIO18 (BCM) for the center output, and GPIO27 (BCM) for the right output, polling each pin every 50 ms with usleep(50000), printing the current states to the console in the format “Left: %d, Center: %d, Right: %d”, checking the return value of every library API call and, on any failure, printing an error message to stderr and exiting with a non‑zero status, and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that terminates the driver library and releases all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads a TTP226 8‑channel digital touch sensor configured for direct GPIO output and logs each channel’s state, using the GPIO bus and connecting OUT1‑OUT8 to BCM GPIO pins 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9 respectively; the program must poll the eight lines every 100 ms and print to the console a timestamped line showing the binary state (0 or 1) of each channel, must check the return values of all driver calls for opening the chip, requesting the lines and reading their values and print descriptive error messages to stderr when any call fails, must handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform a graceful shutdown, and must ensure that all resources such as line handles and the chip are properly released on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads a TTP226 8-channel digital touch sensor connected on the GPIO bus, configuring the eight sensor output pins OUT1‑OUT8 as Broadcom GPIO 2‑9 inputs with pull‑down resistors, initializing the driver library and checking the return value to abort with an error message if initialization fails, then entering a loop that calls the library’s API function with a 100 000‑microsecond (100 ms) sampling interval, validating the return of each API call and aborting with a diagnostic on any failure, printing to the console for each sample a line such as “[+1234 ms] CH1=0 CH2=1 … CH8=0”, and installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so that the loop can exit cleanly and the library’s API call is always invoked during shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads two Texas Instruments TMAG5110 Hall‑Effect Latch sensors connected on the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 OUT wired to BCM GPIO4 and sensor 2 OUT wired to BCM GPIO5, and logs each sensor’s state as HIGH or LOW to the console every 500 ms; the implementation must verify that the driver library initializes correctly and that the GPIO pins are configured in the proper mode, treat the sensor outputs as open‑drain with external pull‑up resistors (so an unasserted output reads HIGH and a magnet‑detected assertion reads LOW), handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform clean resource release and ensure the driver library is terminated on all exit paths, and be compiled with the command `gcc -Wall -o hall_effect hall_effect.c -lthe driver library -lrt`.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads an 8‑channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor array connected via GPIO, using the eight sensor channels mapped to BCM pins 2, 3, 4, 17, 27, 22, 10, 9 (physical pins 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 15, 19, 21), configuring each line as an input with bias disabled, polls the state of all channels every 50 ms, and writes to the console a CSV line for each poll containing an ISO‑8601 timestamp followed by the eight channel states; the program must check every driver call for failure, handle the situation where the library cannot open the device or request any of the lines, install a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl‑C triggers a graceful shutdown, and on all exit paths ensure that every line request and the chip resource are properly released.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls an Omron D7E‑1 tilt sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s output wired to GPIO4 (BCM pin 7), configuring the pin as an input with the internal pull‑up resistor enabled; the program must print a startup banner, then enter a loop that reads the pin every 100 ms, checking the return value of the library’s API call and exiting with an error message if the call fails, validating each GPIO read and handling any unexpected errors, and whenever the tilt state changes it must flush stdout and log to the console “Tilted” when the pin reads LOW/0 or “Not Tilted” when it reads HIGH/1; a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) handler must be installed so that the program exits cleanly on interruption and always invokes the library’s API call on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a Silicon Labs Si1145 UV Index and Ambient Light sensor on I2C bus 1, samples the sensor once every second, and on each sample prints the UV index and visible ambient light reading to the console while also appending a line to a CSV file named uv_als_log.csv containing the timestamp, uv_index, and als_visible columns; the program must handle any I2C communication errors gracefully, detect and report a missing sensor or bus errors robustly, and ensure that all resources such as the I2C file descriptor and the log file are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads flow rates from two Sensirion SLF3S‑0600F Liquid Flow Sensors connected on I2C (/dev/i2c‑1) and logs the average flow rate to a file named flow_log.txt every second, while also driving an alarm on GPIO17 (BCM) when the average of the valid sensor readings falls below 0.5 ml/min and keeping the alarm low otherwise; after issuing a start command to each sensor the program must wait 100 ms before taking the first measurement, then perform subsequent reads at 1‑second intervals, validating each measurement with the Sensirion 8‑bit CRC using the documented polynomial and initial value, and on any I2C communication error or CRC failure it must log the error and skip that sensor’s reading for that cycle, and finally it must handle a clean shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by releasing the GPIO line, closing the I2C file descriptor and the log file.
pinned_library: libgpiod (GPIO) and Linux I2C character-device API (i2c-dev ioctl on /dev/i2c-1)

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously polls a KY-033 Obstacle Avoidance Sensor Module connected on the GPIO bus, using the sensor output on GPIO4 (BCM pin 7) configured as an input with the internal pull‑up resistor enabled, sampling every 50 ms; the program must initialize the driver library and verify success, printing an error to stderr and returning a non‑zero code if initialization fails, record each detection (the sensor drives the line LOW when an obstacle is within the threshold and HIGH otherwise) in a circular buffer of 100 entries overwriting the oldest when full, emit an alert to stdout on every detection, and on receipt of SIGINT release all driver resources, then dump the entire buffer in chronological order to stdout with human‑readable timestamps before exiting cleanly, while ensuring no deprecated APIs are used.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 running the 64‑bit Bookworm OS that interfaces with an Omron D7S vibration sensor over I2C (/dev/i2c-1) using GPIO2 (BCM) for SDA and GPIO3 (BCM) for SCL at up to 400 kHz, switches the sensor to the appropriate mode and then waits up to one second for it to become active, after which it polls the acceleration registers every 500 ms to obtain X, Y and Z values, appends each sample to a CSV file named fan_health.csv with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and a header row written only when the file is newly created, checks the return value of every I2C system call and, on any read, write or ioctl failure, prints a diagnostic message to stderr and simply retries on the next loop iteration without crashing, aborts with an error message and exit if the sensor does not become active within the one‑second window, and handles SIGINT and SIGTERM by cleanly closing the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file before exiting, running continuously until interrupted by the user.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces two Keywish KY-032 Infrared Obstacle Avoidance sensors on the GPIO bus, connecting sensor 1 OUT to GPIO23 (BCM), sensor 2 OUT to GPIO24 (BCM), and driving an LED (anode) on GPIO25 (BCM) through a 220‑330 Ω resistor to ground, polling the sensor outputs every 100 ms, turning the LED on immediately when either sensor reads LOW (active‑LOW indicating an obstacle within roughly 10 cm) and turning it off only when both sensors read HIGH, verifying the driver initialization and checking the return code of every library API call, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released via the appropriate library call on every exit path, including handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a conveyor belt using two E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensors connected via GPIO, with sensor 1 OUT wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and sensor 2 OUT wired to GPIO18 (BCM); the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, validate each sensor read, and consider a stall confirmed only when both sensors read LOW (0) continuously for at least 2 seconds, then record a timestamped entry for each confirmed stall in a file named stall_log.txt while avoiding duplicate entries for the same stall event, handling any file I/O errors that may occur, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released when the process receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with the Texas Instruments TMAG5170‑Q1 I2C 3D Hall‑Effect sensor on I2C bus 1, configures the sensor for continuous‑conversion mode with all three axes enabled and a 50 mT range, then reads the X, Y, and Z magnetic field values every 100 ms in an infinite loop until the user terminates the program with Ctrl‑C, logging each reading to a CSV file named magnetic_log.csv with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and writing a header row if the file is newly created, while checking every I2C read and write return code and handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions by printing error messages to stderr and continuing operation, and finally registering a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C handle, closing the CSV file, and invoking the sensor’s library cleanup call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that runs as a daemon and continuously polls the SEN0193 Water Level Sensor (digital output) connected to the GPIO bus on pin GPIO23 (BCM numbering), using a pull‑down resistor on the input to keep the line low when dry, reading the sensor every 2 seconds and generating an alert whenever a logic HIGH is detected; on each detection the program must print an alert message to stdout and append a line to a file named flood_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS ALERT: Water detected”, while also checking that the driver library initializes correctly and, if a GPIO read fails, logging an error entry to the same file and scheduling an automatic re‑initialization attempt after 60 seconds; the daemon must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to release all resources cleanly before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Bookworm or later that reads the RPM from a Melexis MLX90217 Hall‑effect sensor connected to the GPIO bus, with the sensor output wired to physical pin 7 (BCM GPIO4), by configuring the pin as an input with the internal pull‑up resistor enabled and counting rising‑edge pulses using GPIO interrupts; the program must count pulses in a one‑second window using an atomic add for the pulse counter, compute the revolutions per minute, and log one sample per second to a file named rpm_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS <rpm>” while also printing the same line to stdout, flushing the file after each write; it must check every driver‑library call and the file‑open call for errors, exiting with a diagnostic message on failure, but if the sensor is absent or not rotating it should log an RPM of 0 instead of aborting; finally, the program must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that disable the timer and alert callback, close the log file, and invoke the library’s cleanup API call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses two Melexis MLX90217 unipolar Hall‑effect sensors connected on the GPIO bus in an interrupt‑driven quadrature configuration, with Sensor A wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and Sensor B to GPIO27 (BCM) and hardware pull‑up resistors providing the required 90° electrical offset, to detect the direction of rotation and log each clockwise or counter‑clockwise event to a file named rotation_log.txt using millisecond‑precision timestamps formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS.mmm”; the implementation must employ the driver’s edge‑triggered alerts via the library’s API call for interrupt handling (without using any other driver library), maintain a quadrature state machine that tracks the previous state to infer direction, protect the shared state between the ISR and the main thread with a mutex, have the main loop wait on a condition variable or sleep rather than busy‑wait, check all error paths including each of the three library’s API call() invocations and the file open operation, and install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that performs a graceful shutdown by flushing and closing the log file and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the GPIO bus to monitor a SainSmart TTP223B digital capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO23 (physical pin 16, BCM 23) and to drive an LED on GPIO18 (physical pin 12, BCM 18) with an appropriate current‑limiting resistor, polling the sensor every 50 ms so that the LED is illuminated only while the sensor is actively touched; the program must open the GPIO chip, request the input line for the sensor and the output line for the LED, check the return status of every driver call including chip opening, line requests, reads and writes, handle the situation where the GPIO chip is unavailable, log startup, shutdown, each touch event and any errors to the system syslog using openlog/syslog, and install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that perform a graceful shutdown by turning the LED off and releasing all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads touch input from a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s OUT line on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) to capture rising‑edge events and toggles an LED attached to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) on each detected touch; the program must employ the line event interface to wait for rising edges rather than polling, apply a software debounce of approximately 50 ms after each rising‑edge detection, initialize the LED line as an output and drive it LOW at startup, verify the result of every driver call (chip open, line request, event wait, read, write) and print clear error messages to stderr when a call fails, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by gracefully releasing all driver resources (lines and chip) before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls two SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensors on the GPIO bus—sensor 1 connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO17 (BCM)—with a 50 ms loop to debounce, drives LED 1 on GPIO27 (BCM) and LED 2 on GPIO22 (BCM) such that each LED is lit while its corresponding sensor is touched (sensors are active‑high digital outputs), records every touch and release event in a 100‑entry in‑RAM circular buffer storing the sensor pin number, a Unix timestamp, and the new state while maintaining an overflow counter, checks the return value of every API call and prints a diagnostic to stderr on any failure, handles SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that turns off both LEDs, calls the required API cleanup function, and on shutdown prints the full contents of the log buffer together with the overflow count to stdout.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the ambient light level from a BH1750 I2C light sensor on the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1), waiting approximately 120 ms after initiating a conversion before reading the 2‑byte result, and then scales the brightness of an APA102 LED strip connected via the SPI bus (/dev/spidev0.0) proportionally to the measured illumination; the APA102 data stream must be constructed with a 32‑bit zero start frame, followed by one 32‑bit LED frame per LED containing the documented brightness, blue, green, and red fields, and terminated with a 32‑bit end frame, transmitted at a 1 MHz SPI clock, while implementing robust error handling for all I/O operations, sensor‑absent scenarios, and bus errors, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT the program gracefully turns off all LEDs and closes every opened file descriptor.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads ambient light from up to three BH1750 I2C light sensors on I2C bus 1, averaging the valid readings, and uses the result to smoothly adjust the global brightness of an APA102 RGB LED strip driven over hardware SPI, with the APA102 data line (MOSI) connected to GPIO10 (BCM) and the clock line (SCLK) to GPIO11 (BCM); the program must wait approximately 180 ms after initiating a conversion before reading the two‑byte result from each sensor, attempt to open both possible BH1750 addresses and gracefully skip any sensor that is not present, check all driver initialization and I2C/SPI calls for errors and handle missing sensors or bus errors without crashing, fade the strip’s brightness to the newly computed target over 500 ms, loop indefinitely with a 100 ms delay between cycles, and install a SIGINT handler that on termination turns off the LED strip, closes all I2C handles, closes the SPI handle, and terminates the driver library on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously reads ambient light from a VEML7700 ambient light sensor on the I2C bus, applies gamma‑corrected scaling to determine a brightness level for a WS2812B LED strip, and drives the strip by bit‑banging the data line on GPIO18 (BCM) without using any deprecated or external driver libraries, toggling at the required high frequency (approximately 800 kHz) or falling back to a simple threshold‑based on/off scheme if precise timing cannot be achieved; the program must run in an infinite loop with a 200 ms pause between iterations, print the current lux reading and the computed brightness value to stdout each cycle, retry any I2C communication errors up to three times with a 100 ms delay between attempts, log an error and continue if all retries fail, and install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that gracefully release the GPIO line, close the I2C file descriptor, and turn off the LED strip before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the GPIO bus to interface a KY‑026 flame sensor (digital output, active‑low) on BCM GPIO4, a buzzer on BCM GPIO17 and an LED on BCM GPIO18, performing a startup self‑test in which the LED blinks 500 ms on/500 ms off twice while the flame sensor is read five times at 100 ms intervals, and if any of those reads indicate a persistent LOW (flame detected on all five samples) the program must signal an error by blinking the LED rapidly (100 ms on/100 ms off for five cycles) and sounding the buzzer with a short‑short‑long‑short pattern of 200 ms, 200 ms, 600 ms, 200 ms repeated three times, then exit with code 1; after a successful self‑test the main loop polls the flame sensor every 50 ms, and when a LOW is observed the buzzer and LED are turned on continuously until a subsequent read returns HIGH, at which point they are turned off, while all events (flame detected, flame cleared, any errors) are logged with timestamps; every call that requests a line or reads/writes a value must be checked and any failure handled gracefully with clear error messages, and on normal termination or receipt of SIGINT a signal handler must clean up all GPIO lines before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the ambient light from a BH1750 digital light sensor on the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) once every second, stores the last 60 lux readings in a circular buffer, computes the average lux of the buffer, and blinks an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) with a 50 % duty‑cycle square wave whose frequency varies proportionally from 0.5 Hz in darkness to 5 Hz at bright levels (1000 + lux); if a sensor read fails the program must print an error, skip that sample, and attempt a new read on the next loop iteration, and on program termination via Ctrl‑C it must catch SIGINT, cleanly release the GPIO (unexport) and close the I2C file descriptor, using only standard POSIX and Linux kernel headers and no external libraries.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the GPIO bus to bit‑bang a 74HC595 shift register which drives a common‑cathode seven‑segment display, configuring GPIO17 (BCM) as the data line, GPIO18 (BCM) as the clock line, and GPIO27 (BCM) as the latch line, initializing the driver library and setting all three pins as outputs, implementing a robust shift‑out routine that sends 8 bits MSB‑first with proper clock and latch timing, mapping the 74HC595 outputs Q0 through Q7 to segments a, b, c, d, e, f, g, and dp respectively (with dp unused) so that the pattern for digit ‘5’ is shifted out, then repeatedly blinking this digit on the display with a 500 ms on period and a 500 ms off period, including error checking for the line requests and ensuring that on program exit all GPIO lines are released and the chip is cleanly closed.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (any model with a 40‑pin GPIO header) that blinks an LED connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11, BCM numbering) with a 2‑second period (1 second on, 1 second off) using the library’s call() function with a 1‑second timeout, while simultaneously waiting for a falling‑edge event from a momentary push button wired to GPIO18 (physical pin 12, BCM) configured as an input with a pull‑up and event detection; the program must request the LED line as an output initially set low, request the button line as an input with the specified pull‑up and edge detection, open GPIO chip 0, and on detection of the falling edge it must stop the blinking immediately, turn the LED off, print a message indicating the button press, and then exit cleanly after releasing all resources (releasing the lines and closing the chip) on every exit path, including handling SIGINT so that Ctrl‑C also triggers graceful termination; robust error checking must be performed for every driver call (chip open, line request, event request, line set/get), and the source should be compiled with gcc -o blink_button blink_button.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that blinks an LED connected to the GPIO bus on GPIO5 (BCM, physical pin 29) with a periodic delay of 750 ms on and 750 ms off, setting GPIO5 as an output, printing “LED ON” and “LED OFF” to stdout with each state change and flushing after each print, initializing the driver library and checking for failure and exiting with a non‑zero code if initialization fails, and handling SIGINT gracefully by cleanly turning off the LED, terminating the driver library, releasing all driver resources, and exiting with code 0, while using only the driver library’s API calls for pin control and either its timing function or a time_sleep equivalent so that the program runs correctly in both real and emulated Raspberry Pi environments.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the GPIO bus to control an LED and a button, wiring the LED anode to GPIO24 (BCM, physical pin 18) through a 330 Ω resistor to ground and connecting the button between GPIO22 (BCM, physical pin 15) and 3.3 V with a 10 kΩ pull‑down to ground (or the internal pull‑down if available); configure GPIO24 as an output initially low and GPIO22 as an input with pull‑down, then continuously monitor the button, and while the button is held the program must blink the LED with a 500 ms on / 500 ms off pattern, turning the LED off immediately when the button is released and keeping it off until the next press, running indefinitely until terminated by Ctrl‑C, and for every driver library call (chip open, line get, direction set, value read/write) the code must check the return status and print a descriptive error message to stderr, handling cases where the device is not found or lines are busy, and on program exit—including receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM—must gracefully release all driver resources such as lines and the chip.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously drives a common‑cathode RGB LED attached to the GPIO bus, with the red channel on GPIO24 (physical pin 18, BCM), green on GPIO23 (physical pin 16, BCM) and blue on GPIO18 (physical pin 12, BCM), using software PWM implemented in a simple timing loop (no hardware PWM) at 100 Hz (10 ms period) for each channel, generating random intensity values from 0 to 100 for each colour using rand() seeded with time(NULL) and changing the colour randomly every 100 ms; the program must check the library's API call() for each line, check the library's API call() for each line, check the library's API call() for each line and report descriptive error messages on failure, employ a busy‑wait PWM loop with clock_nanosleep for sub‑millisecond precision (no sleep calls shorter than 1 ms), run indefinitely until the user presses Ctrl+C, and on receipt of SIGINT invoke a signal handler that cleanly releases all GPIO lines and exits, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls an Adafruit LSM303DLHC accelerometer on I2C bus 1 at 10 Hz, computes the total G‑force magnitude, and when that magnitude exceeds a configurable threshold (default 2.0 G, settable with a ‑t command‑line argument) triggers an impact interrupt by setting GPIO17 (BCM numbering) as an output and pulsing it HIGH for 50 ms, while also logging the timestamped accelerometer data to a file named impact_log.txt; the program must check the result of every I2C read and write operation, handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors, and ensure that on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM—it cleanly releases all resources such as the I2C handle, the GPIO pin, and any driver state.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads ambient light and color data from an Analog Devices ADPD188BI optical sensor on I2C bus 1, samples the sensor every 500 ms, combines the ALS LSB and MSB into a 16‑bit unsigned value, and logs each timestamped reading of ALS, red, green and blue channels to a CSV file named color_log.csv with a header row; the program must also control an LED connected to GPIO18 (BCM) using hardware PWM so that brighter ambient light increases the LED brightness, handle any I2C errors such as failed writes, reads or a missing sensor by writing an error message to stderr and retrying after a 100 ms delay, and implement signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, turns off the LED and closes the CSV file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the Adafruit FXOS8700CQ 6‑Axis Accelerometer/Magnetometer over I2C bus 1 at a 50 ms interval, first verifying the WHO_AM_I identifier on startup and aborting with a clear error message if it does not match, then placing the device in standby, configuring the sensor for a ±2 g range, and finally activating it for a 200 Hz output data rate; each loop must compute the acceleration magnitude from the three axes, and whenever the magnitude exceeds a defined impact threshold the program should append a line to “impact_log.txt” containing the current timestamp and the raw x, y, z values and the computed magnitude formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,x,y,z,magnitude” with three decimal places, while checking the return value of every I2C call, printing a diagnostic to stderr on read errors and continuing the loop rather than crashing, and the application must handle SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) by gracefully closing the I2C handle, invoking the appropriate library shutdown call, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces over I2C bus 1 with a GY-50 L3G4200D gyroscope, performs a 100‑sample stationary calibration at startup to compute X, Y and Z zero‑rate offsets, then continuously reads angular velocity, applies the offsets, and logs the calibrated X, Y, Z values together with ISO‑8601 timestamps to a file named gyro_log.txt at a 20 Hz rate (50 ms period), appending an alert line to the same log whenever any axis exceeds 50 dps and also printing a warning to stderr for the same condition; the program must verify the result of every open, ioctl, read and write call, detect sensor absence by reading the WHO_AM_I register and confirming the documented value, handle any I2C bus errors, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the I2C file descriptor and the log file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads data from a GY-51 LSM303DLHC accelerometer and magnetometer connected on I2C bus 1, samples the sensors every 100 ms, computes a tilt‑compensated heading, and logs each sample with a timestamp, the heading, the three‑axis acceleration in g, and the three‑axis magnetic field in gauss to a file named compass_log.txt, adding a CSV header when the file is created; the program must check the result of every I2C operation and handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error, and it must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handles and terminates the driver library.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples two STMicroelectronics IMP23ABSU Ultrasonic MEMS Microphone sensors connected on I2C bus 1 at a 10 ms sampling interval, reads 16‑bit signed audio samples from each sensor, timestamps each pair of samples using CLOCK_REALTIME, computes the time‑difference‑of‑arrival (TDOA) between the two channels, and appends a line to a CSV‑formatted file named audio_log.dat with the columns sec,nsec,sensor1,sensor2,tdoa; the implementation must verify that all driver library initialization and I2C communication calls succeed, and if a sensor is absent or the bus fails it must gracefully skip that sample and retry, while a SIGINT signal handler must guarantee clean release of I2C handles, closure of the log file, and termination of the driver library on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads gyroscope and accelerometer data from an Analog Devices ADIS16488A IMU over SPI0 CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) using a 1 MHz SPI clock in mode 3 (CPOL = 1, CPHA = 1) with 16‑bit words, respecting a stall time of at least 40 µs between the read request and the data transfer, sampling every 100 ms and attaching millisecond‑precision timestamps; each read consists of a 16‑bit command word whose MSB is 0 followed by the 7‑bit register address and the data are returned on the subsequent 16‑bit transfer, and the raw values must be converted using a gyroscope sensitivity of 0.005 deg/sec/LSB and an accelerometer sensitivity of 0.00025 g/LSB before being logged to a file named imu_data.csv with a header row “timestamp,gyro_x,gyro_y,gyro_z,accel_x,accel_y,accel_z”, while checking the API call return values and the fopen return value, logging any API call that returns less than 0 to stderr and skipping that sample; the program must install a cleanup() helper with atexit() to close the SPI handle, the CSV file and terminate the driver on all exit paths, handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, and use a non‑blocking delay that checks a running flag every few milliseconds so signals are processed promptly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that communicates with an Analog Devices ADIS16448 IMU over SPI bus 0 using chip‑select CS0 on GPIO8 (BCM) in SPI mode 3 with a maximum clock of 1 MHz, reads the gyroscope and accelerometer registers using the single‑register read protocol (send the 8‑bit register address with bit 7 set in the first 16‑bit SPI cycle and capture the 16‑bit data response in the second cycle), applies the gyro scale of 0.02 dps/LSB and accel scale of 0.00025 g/LSB, and logs the six values (gyroscope X, Y, Z and accelerometer X, Y, Z) to the console every 100 ms; the program must include robust error handling for SPI initialization, ioctl transfers, and data reads, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to cleanly release resources by closing the SPI device file and the driver library chip before exiting.
pinned_library: libgpiod for chip-select/GPIO control with the Linux spidev ioctl interface for SPI transfers

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads the gyroscope and accelerometer data from an Analog Devices ADIS16448 IMU over SPI channel 0 using CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM), operating at 1 MHz in SPI Mode 0, and prints the six values (gyro x, y, z and accel x, y, z) to the console every 100 ms; the read sequence must follow the two‑cycle protocol where the first 16‑bit transfer sends the read command (register address with bit 15 set), then after a stall time of at least 40 µs a second 16‑bit transfer sends the documented dummy value to clock out the 16‑bit data, which should be scaled using 0.05 deg/sec per LSB for the gyroscope and 0.00025 g per LSB for the accelerometer, and the implementation must include robust error handling for driver library initialization, SPI opening, and any transfer failures, while also handling a Ctrl‑C interrupt cleanly by closing the SPI handle and invoking the library’s API call() before exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the raw 16‑bit signed accelerometer and gyroscope values from a TDK MPU‑6886 6‑axis IMU over I2C bus 1 every 50 ms and prints those values to the console, checking every I2C system call for errors, retrying any transient read failure up to three times, and handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, while also ensuring that the I2C file descriptor is cleanly closed on all exit paths, including when the program receives a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls an Adafruit ADXL345 accelerometer on I2C bus 1 every 10 ms in full‑resolution mode with a ±2 g range (scale factor 256 LSB/g), verifies that the device ID register returns the documented value and checks the result of every I2C read or write, and when the computed total acceleration magnitude exceeds a 2.5 g threshold it turns on a red LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) for 500 ms, records the event to a file named impact_log.txt with a timestamp and the magnitude together with the X, Y and Z components, and ensures that on normal exit or on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM all resources—including the I2C handle, the LED GPIO, the log file and any driver state—are cleanly released, while also handling sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions according to the verification steps.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that opens I2C bus 1 to communicate with a TDK InvenSense ICM‑20602 IMU, performs burst reads of the six accelerometer bytes and six gyroscope bytes at a 10 Hz rate (every 100 ms), checks the return value of every I2C operation and prints any failures to stderr, timestamps each sample and appends the x, y, z accelerometer and gyroscope values to a file named imu_log.csv, and handles Ctrl +C (SIGINT) gracefully by closing the I2C handle, terminating the driver library, and closing the CSV file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads ambient light from a BH1750 sensor on I2C1 (GPIO2 =SDA, GPIO3 =SCL) using the documented address, waiting at least 120 ms after each trigger before reading the 2‑byte lux result and sampling every 2 seconds, logs a timestamp and the lux value to grow_log.txt, and drives a grow‑light relay on GPIO23 (BCM) so that the relay is activated when the lux reading falls below 150 and deactivated when it is 150 or above, while implementing robust error handling that checks the return codes of every I2C call and of file operations, logs any sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions and simply retries on the next cycle, and ensures that on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM—the program cleanly releases all resources by closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, deactivating the relay, and invoking the appropriate library cleanup call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors weight using a TAL220B load cell with an HX711 amplifier over a bit‑banged GPIO bus, reading HX711 DOUT on GPIO23 (physical pin 16) and HX711 SCK on GPIO24 (physical pin 18), and drives a solenoid lock on GPIO25 (physical pin 22); the program must perform a startup tare by averaging ten 24‑bit two’s‑complement readings (obtained by waiting for DOUT to go LOW, clocking out 24 bits MSB‑first, then one extra clock pulse to select Channel A gain 128), then in the main loop poll the weight every 500 ms, averaging five readings per measurement cycle, apply an optional scale factor, and if the measured weight exceeds a threshold (default 1000 grams, overridable with a --threshold <grams> command‑line argument) activate the solenoid lock by setting GPIO25 HIGH for 200 ms before returning it LOW; each HX711 read must check that DOUT goes LOW within 1 second, logging an error via syslog and retrying up to three times before exiting, and every driver call must be verified for errors; the program should accept optional --scale <factor> and --duration <ms> arguments, log informational and error messages through syslog, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO lines and chips, closes syslog, and ensures the solenoid is set LOW before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Raspberry Pi OS that controls a relay module attached to the GPIO bus on GPIO17 (physical pin 11, BCM numbering) by subscribing to the MQTT topic home/lights/control with QoS 0, connecting to a broker at localhost port 1883 using client ID relay_controller_1 and a clean session, maintaining a 60‑second keep‑alive, and on successful connect logging the event to syslog (facility LOG_USER, tag mqtt_relay) and subscribing to the topic; the program must initialize the GPIO driver, configure GPIO17 as an output and drive it LOW (relay OFF) at startup, then in the main thread run the MQTT client loop, handling incoming payloads as NUL‑terminated strings where the exact values “ON” set GPIO17 HIGH (relay energized) and “OFF” set it LOW (relay de‑energized), logging any empty or invalid payload as an error (syslog LOG_ERR) without changing the relay state, and for every connection, subscription, disconnection, or error event logging the details to syslog, checking all return codes from the driver and MQTT client and reporting failures via syslog while never exiting on transient MQTT errors; on loop errors or unexpected disconnects the program must wait five seconds before attempting to reconnect, and a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must stop the loop, set GPIO17 LOW, disconnect and destroy the MQTT client, clean up the driver library, call the library cleanup function, and close the syslog; the source should be compiled with gcc using optimization level 2 and all warnings enabled, producing an executable named relay_controller.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that moves five hobby servos connected to the GPIO bus to predefined positions by generating a 50 Hz PWM signal (20 ms period) on BCM GPIO 7 for Servo 1, BCM GPIO 8 for Servo 2, BCM GPIO 9 for Servo 3, BCM GPIO 10 for Servo 4, and BCM GPIO 11 for Servo 5, holding each pulse for three seconds; the program must initialize the driver library and verify the return code before use, then output pulse widths constrained between 500 µs and 2500 µs with target values of 1000 µs, 1500 µs, 2000 µs, 500 µs, and 2500 µs respectively for the five servos, and finally cleanly stop the PWM and release all library resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements closed‑loop DC motor speed control for a miniature vehicle using quadrature encoders, driving two DC motors through a DRV8833 H‑bridge on the GPIO bus with PWM and digital signals; use GPIO 17 (BCM) as Motor A PWM (IN1), GPIO 18 as Motor A direction (IN2), GPIO 22 as Motor B PWM (IN3), GPIO 23 as Motor B direction (IN4), read Encoder A phase A on GPIO 4, Encoder A phase B on GPIO 5, Encoder B phase A on GPIO 6, and Encoder B phase B on GPIO 12, run a PI control loop every 100 ms with a 10 kHz PWM frequency, assume 64 ticks per revolution with a single count per rising edge and a 1:1 encoder‑to‑output‑shaft ratio, target 50 RPM for both motors, drive each motor by holding one input pin high and PWM‑modulating the other for forward motion, clamp the PWM duty cycle to the range 0‑255 and implement anti‑windup clamping in the controller, maintain encoder tick counters with atomic operations, detect an encoder stall when zero ticks are observed for more than 2 seconds and print a warning, print the motor RPM and PWM duty cycle each control iteration, check the driver library initialization and ISR registration calls and exit cleanly on any failure, and handle SIGINT by stopping the motors and releasing all resources, ensuring the code compiles cleanly with ‑Wall.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors ambient light using a BH1750 light sensor on I2C bus 1 (using the documented address) and controls a 12 V LED strip through a relay connected to GPIO 17 (BCM, active‑high), polling the sensor every 5 seconds and waiting at least 180 ms after issuing the mode command before reading, logging each sensor reading and any relay state change to a file named chicken_coop_log.txt in the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS: Lux = XXX, Relay = ON/OFF”, activating the relay at dusk when lux falls below 50 and deactivating it at dawn when lux rises above 200 with hysteresis to avoid rapid toggling, implementing comprehensive error handling for driver initialization, I2C communication and file I/O such that any sensor non‑response is logged and the relay is safely turned off, and ensuring that all resources—including the I2C handle, the GPIO pin and the log file—are cleanly released on every exit path, including graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses a GPIO bus to read a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7) as an input and control a 5 V relay on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11) as an output, implementing a touch‑toggled relay with debouncing: each valid touch detection must toggle the relay state only when the sensor reads HIGH both before and after a 50 ms debounce stabilization delay, then wait for the sensor to return LOW before allowing the next toggle (edge detection on touch‑release), with the main loop sleeping 10 ms between iterations; every relay state change must be logged to the console with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and the new state (ON or OFF); the program must check the return value of every the driver library call (the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call) and report any errors to stderr; a SIGINT handler must turn the relay OFF, release the driver library resources, and print an exit message; no MQTT or networking code is to be included.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that monitors water flow using a YF‑S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM numbering) and controls a solenoid valve on GPIO 27 (BCM) via the GPIO bus, implementing a 1‑second ISR debounce timeout on the flow‑sensor pin and sampling the pulse count every second; the program must protect the shared pulse counter with a pthread mutex, log each liters‑per‑minute (LPM) reading and every solenoid state change with timestamps to a file named water_flow.log, initialize the driver library and validate all return codes for each library API call, and if the log file cannot be opened, clean up all initialized resources and exit with a non‑zero status; the solenoid is open (HIGH) by default and must be driven LOW to shut off when the measured flow exceeds 5.0 LPM, reopening only when the flow drops below 4.5 LPM to provide a 0.5 L/min hysteresis, and the program must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by logging the event, returning the solenoid to its safe open state, closing the log file, destroying the mutex, and calling the library’s cleanup API.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that implements a TCP‑driven ingredient dispenser using a load cell and the library’s API call, where the HX711 load cell amplifier is bit‑banged on the GPIO bus with DATA on GPIO 23 (BCM) and SCK on GPIO 24 (BCM) using a 1 µs clock pulse width and timing out if DATA remains HIGH for more than 1000 attempts, while an SG90‑style servo motor is driven via hardware PWM on GPIO 18 (BCM); the program must listen on 127.0.0.1:12345, receive a target weight in grams, open the library’s API call to dispense, wait 1 second for the load cell to stabilize after dispensing begins, read the actual weight, calibrate the reading using a known weight and a calibration_factor read from config.ini (falling back to defaults if the file is missing or malformed), map the target weight to the 1000‑2000 µs pulse width range required by the API call, send the actual weight back to the client, and append each dispensing event—including date, time, target weight, actual weight, and any error message—as a JSON object to dispensing_log.json; robust error handling must cover initialization of the driver, HX711 communication timeouts (sensor absent or not ready), API call control failures, file I/O problems, and network errors, and signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM must ensure a clean shutdown of GPIO, sockets, and the library’s API call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4/5 (using the 40‑pin header) that lets a user adjust the angle of a hobby servo such as an SG90 via keyboard input, driving the servo on GPIO18 (BCM 18, physical pin 12) with hardware PWM on the GPIO bus at a 50 Hz frequency (20 ms period); the program must start the servo at 90° (1500 µs pulse width), increase the angle by 10° for each ‘+’ key and decrease by 10° for each ‘‑’ key, clamp the angle between 0° and 180° and ensure the computed pulse widths stay within the 500‑2500 µs range, print the current angle after every change, read keys in raw terminal mode so no Enter is required, use the library's API call() to set the pulse width (checking its return value and printing any error to stderr before exiting with a non‑zero status), and on receiving ‘q’ or a SIGINT must stop PWM pulses on GPIO18, invoke the library's API call() one final time, restore the terminal settings and properly save and restore the driver library state even on unexpected exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors the RPM of a conveyor‑belt motor using an A3144 Hall‑effect sensor and a two‑pole magnet mounted on the motor shaft, connecting the sensor to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM numbering) with the internal pull‑up bias flag enabled; the program must use edge‑triggered event detection on the rising edge (the two‑pole magnet yields one pulse per revolution), apply a 2 ms debounce window to reject contact bounce and double‑edge noise, count pulses with a monotonic clock (clock_gettime with CLOCK_MONOTONIC), compute the motor RPM every 5 seconds, and after each interval write a line to motor_rpm.log in CSV format containing an ISO 8601 timestamp and the RPM value to two decimal places (flushed after every write) while also printing the current RPM to stdout; it must check the library’s API call return values, printing clear diagnostics to stderr and exiting with a non‑zero status on any failure, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by stopping the main loop, releasing the GPIO line, closing the chip and the log file, and exiting cleanly.
